https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/16/hala.text: Menü Kereső Halálos buszbaleset: különgépet küld Magyarországra Donald Tusk Külföld Drónfotón az árokba borult busz mentése – Fotó: Máthé Zoltán / MTI Barnóczki Brigitta Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Úgy döntöttem, hogy egy különgépet küldök Magyarországra, amelyen a Külügyminisztérium és az egészségügyi szolgálatok képviselői is utaznak. Minden sérült megkapja a szükséges orvosi és konzuli segítséget ebben a nehéz pillanatban, írta az X-en Donald Tusk lengyel miniszterelnök. Egy másik posztban azt írta, telefonon tárgyalt Magyar Péterrel, aki neki is részvétét nyilvánította ki a tragédia miatt. Lengyelország budapesti nagykövetsége napközben forródrótot hozott létre a baleset halálos áldozatainak és sérültjeinek hozzátartozói számára. Magyar Péter vasárnap 13 óra után nem sokkal posztolt arról a Facebookon, hogy telefonon tárgyalt Donald Tusk lengyel miniszterelnökkel, neki is részvétét fejezte ki, és azt írta, a lengyel kormányfő megköszönte a magyar mentőalakulatok segítségét. Donald Tusk az X-en posztolt a Magyar Péterrel folytatott beszélgetésről, azt írta, a magyar miniszterelnök részvétét fejezte ki az áldozatok családjainak és egész Lengyelországnak, és biztosította, hogy továbbra is mindent meg fog tenni annak érdekében, hogy segítsen mindazoknak, akiket a tragikus esemény érint. Egy zarándoklat résztvevői utaztak hazafelé azon a lengyel turistabuszon, ami egyelőre tisztázatlan okból letért az útról és árokba borult az M3-as autópályán vasárnap éjjel 1 órakor, a rendőrség hivatalos tájékoztatása szerint a balesetben tizenketten meghaltak . A busz utasai lengyel állampolgárok voltak – erősítette meg varsói sajtóértekezletén Maciej Wewiór külügyi szóvivő, aki azt mondta, hét sérült állapota „nagyon súlyos”, további mintegy 40 személy könnyebb sérüléseket szenvedett, írja az MTI. A kelet-lengyelországi Rzeszówban működő Kárpátvajdasági hivatal szóvivője a Gazeta Wyborcza szerint azt mondta, vajdaságból indult zarándoklat résztvevői hazafelé tartottak Bosznia-Hercegovinából, a busz sofőrjét még a nap folyamán őrizetbe veszik, részletek ebben a cikkben. https://www.politico.eu/article/21-thing.text: This was supposed to be an EU summit about the EU’s long-term budget. But things are never easy for EU leaders, and world events have a nasty habit of making their way onto the itinerary. That meant this European Council had a lot more on the agenda than the last handful of summits, at least: Energy, migration, enlargement, Ukraine, and more besides were covered — and very little, if anything, was decided. Have FOMO because you weren’t there? Don’t worry, we’ve got you covered. Here’s POLITICO’s rapid roundup of what we learned at the European Council. Advertisement Advertisement 1) Energy stole the show right out of the gate The summit’s first major clash came Thursday morning, with EU leaders split over whether to delay ETS2, the bloc’s second phase of carbon pricing, to address high energy prices, triggering a three-hour-long standoff. Italy and Greece joined the Visegrád Four — Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia — in calling for a delay, a push rejected by the majority of countries. The debate dragged on, delaying lunch (spare a thought for our hungry leaders!) and leading to the cancellation of a press conference on Thursday night. 2) Budget negotiations are a marathon… Negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget were expected to be one of the summit’s most contentious topics. But they were a nothingburger, with most leaders repeating positions they have held for months. The summit brought them no closer to a breakthrough. Many countries, of course, want a smaller budget, with Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson telling reporters that his country is “not an ATM for the EU.” Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever, meanwhile, said he had no choice but to be frugal at the European level, arguing he is used to tightening his belt at home because his wife is Dutch. Think of Bart next time your Dutch friends ask you to pay them back for that coffee. Advertisement Advertisement 3) … and a sprint European Council President António Costa is still aiming to get a budget deal before the end of the year, according to two EU officials. He announced that leaders will hold a special summit at the end of November to try and make progress (and there’s a December summit too). But that timing leaves them up against the clock to reach a deal by year’s end. See you all back here on Nov. 26! 4) EU leaders may need to bring extra luggage next time If leaders do hope to agree on the EU’s long-term budget this year, they should prepare for long negotiations in November and December. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested the pre-Christmas summit could last longer than the scheduled two days. “For the December summit, we should pack a few more shirts than usual,” he said. Gulp! 5) Your next holiday to Cyprus might be a little easier Cypriot President Nikos Christodoulides told reporters he hopes EU leaders will discuss his country’s bid to join the Schengen travel zone at the December summit. “All technical preparations have already been completed, and we hope that the matter will be discussed by the relevant council in December so that the final political decisions can be made,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement 6) Rose-colored glasses have come off when it comes to Costa European Council President António Costa drew the ire of some leaders over his handling of negotiations to curb high energy prices, which had become a “mess,” three EU diplomats told POLITICO, with another two diplomats saying that leaders were fuming at Costa for allowing talks to go off the rails. 7) Drink (a little) less beer to help Ukraine Ahead of the summit, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs told reporters that supporting Ukraine costs each European the equivalent of one beer a year. “That one beer is just a cost [for EU citizens]. There, it’s a cost of life. We drink less, their lives are saved,” he said. “Simple as that.” He didn’t say whether he meant a beer bought in Stockholm or Prague. As anyone in Belgium knows, not all beers are created equal — or cost the same. 8) The EU Parliament wants you to know it matters too The European Parliament’s two lead negotiators on the EU budget made the rounds of the press room to make sure journalists heard their views. Siegfried Mureșan (of the European People’s Party) and Carla Tavares (Socialists and Democrats) both stressed that the Parliament’s position is important. Meanwhile, European Parliament President Roberta Metsola joined leaders for the first part of the summit. Metsola said she had made it clear to them that “the Parliament is not a rubber-stamp and never will be.” Advertisement Advertisement 9) Talking China (without mentioning China) Leaders discussed trade imbalances (read: China) over lunch on Thursday and welcomed the deal the European Commission struck with China last week to curb imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles. Czech PM Andrej Babiš even went so far as to call the deal “fantastic.” POLITICO scooped that the European Commission is expected to work on trade measures tackling imports of chemicals and industrial machinery in an effort to protect European industry from unfair Chinese competition. 10) New bromance brewing Hungarian PM Peter Magyar posted a late-night selfie with Dutch PM Rob Jetten on social media after day one of the summit. The two were all smiles and “tired, but not sad”, as Magyar put it in his tweet. In reaction to the tweet, Jetten told reporters, “We are more or less of the same generation and a tad more direct and pragmatic than some colleagues in the European Council, so there’s a click.” We started at 7:30 this morning in Brussels. The second shift begins after 10 PM, with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten @MinPres . Tired, but not sad. pic.twitter.com/dmtSMbqG4m — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) October 15, 2026 11) Back to the castle António Costa announced that another competitiveness summit at Alden Biesen castle in the Belgian countryside will take place in February 2027, three EU diplomats told POLITICO. Leaders already visited the castle earlier this year, and they clearly loved the Belgian countryside so much they want to return (or Costa is forcing them to go). Advertisement Advertisement 12) Still reeling from Ceuta Ahead of Friday’s talks, 16 EU leaders met to discuss migration over breakfast (before discussing migration over lunch with everyone else). According to one EU diplomat, leaders broadly agreed that the EU should be able to suspend asylum applications when faced with a sudden influx of migrants that may have been engineered on purpose. But would that mean the EU will implement pushbacks (which are banned under EU law)? 13) Denmark, Italy and Poland want to be tougher on migration The three leaders joined forces to argue that migration is a concern for many EU citizens and is contributing to rising crime rates. That caused a delay to an already shockingly long summit. 14) There were some agreements Italy’s Giorgia Meloni and Spain’s Pedro Sánchez found some time on the sidelines of the summit to chat about Rome’s restrictions on Spanish nationals sparked by the Ceuta crisis. Plus, France and Germany said they had struck a deal to favor European-made cars under the Industrial Accelerator Act in exchange for weakening a 2035 vehicle emissions target, ending months of wrangling between the bloc’s two biggest economies. 15) EU leaders get the good stuff to eat Thursday’s lunch menu featured a “full-flavored vegetable jus.” Not a little flavor, not a medium amount of flavor, but the full flavor. Then on Friday there was a “rich jus”. There was also a Champagne sauce. Only the best for our leaders! Advertisement 16) The same can’t be said for reporters Some POLITICO journalists lamented the lack of vegetarian options at the Council canteen. Pray for us. 17) No harsh words from EU to Zelenskyy At a press conference on Friday afternoon, Volodymyr Zelenskyy was asked whether EU leaders had expressed annoyance at his recent tone toward U.S. President Donald Trump. The question followed reports that some capitals were frustrated with him and worried he was further riling the White House. But it was all love from Zelenskyy, who said there had been no harsh words during his time in the summit room. “I heard from my European colleagues support and only support, and I’m grateful for this,” he said. 18) No hugs for Fico As Zelenskyy entered the European Council building, he was seen hugging and kissing fellow leaders — with one exception: Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico received no hug. That may well have been because Slovakia is preparing to revive a dormant cooperation forum with Moscow. 19) 20M Ukrainians could flee to Europe if Russia wins war Zelenskyy issued a stark warning to Europe: if Russia wins the war, as many as 20 million Ukrainians could be forced to flee to Europe. Over 4 million Ukrainians already live in EU countries under temporary protection status, according to Eurostat . 20) EU leaders have forgotten about Britain … or have they? There was plenty of talk across the Channel this week about the U.K. potentially rejoining the bloc, but the subject did not come up at the summit, even with an EU-U.K. summit due next month. EU leaders have more pressing issues on their minds. Advertisement Still, some had things to say about the U.K.’s relationship with the EU. Foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said “all our friends are welcome to join,” naming Britain alongside Canada, Norway and Iceland as partners seeking closer ties. Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs suggested the U.K. “should come back to the family,” although he also said that Russia “had its hands on Brexit.” 21) At POLITICO, we save the best for last Covering European Councils often involves a lot of waiting around, but during this summit conditions were a little tougher because of a phantom farter among reporters waiting for Zelenskyy’s press conference. POLITICO went viral in Brussels’ diplomatic and journalistic circles for reporting the hard facts on our live blog. While this summit’s agenda was packed, in the end not many concrete decisions were taken. Some might say the summit was a load of hot air.

https://www.wnd.com/2026/10/perfidious-l.text: A perfidious lie: Why Israel’s action cannot be considered ‘genocide’ By Michael Brown October 9, 2026 I write these words from Poland, where 90% of Poland’s Jews – 3 million out of 3.3 million – were slaughtered during World War II. That is what genocide looks like. In stark contrast, roughly 70,000 of Gaza’s 2.3 million residents were killed during Israel’s war with Hamas, amounting to approximately 3% of the population. And that figure includes enemy combatants. Yet the same word, genocide, used for the systematic, intentional murder of 90% of Poland’s Jews – and two-thirds of Europe’s Jews as a whole – is being used to describe Israel’s war with Hamas. How can this be? And where is the moral equivalence? Recently, more than 6,000 public figures signed an open letter denouncing the Gaza genocide libel, and while the acute suffering of the people of Gaza must not be minimized, these public figures are correct: it is grossly inaccurate and even immoral to label their suffering a “genocide.” This does not mean that the IDF always acted justly and morally or that several prominent Israeli leaders have not made inexcusable statements. Nor does debunking the genocide lie minimize the very real and acute suffering of the Gazan population. A tragic death is a tragic death. But tragic deaths in war do not equate with a genocide. Get the hottest, most important news stories on the Internet – delivered FREE to your inbox as soon as they break! Take just 30 seconds and sign up for WND's Email News Alerts! Consider first the numbers involved. The Holocaust killed 6 million of Europe’s 9 million Jews (67%); in Poland, 90% of Jews were murdered. The Armenian genocide (1915–1916) killed 664,000–1.2 million of roughly 1.5 million Armenians (44–80%). The Rwandan genocide (1994) killed 500,000–1 million people, overwhelmingly Tutsi, in just 100 days, out of roughly 1 million Tutsi in Rwanda. Under the Khmer Rouge (1975–1979), nearly 2 million Cambodians died – roughly 25–30% of the country’s population. Israel’s war with Hamas resulted in the deaths of approximately 70,000 people, representing 3% of the population. How can this possibly be referred to as a “genocide”? We are often told that the answer is “intent,” the allegation being that it was the intent of the IDF (and/or the Israeli government) to wipe out the Gazan population, just as the Nazis planned to wipe out Europe’s Jews. This, too, is categorically false. To the contrary, Israel took extraordinary measures to minimize civilian casualties, despite Hamas embedding itself in the civilian population and Hamas combatants wearing civilian clothing. Just two months into the war (as of Dec. 8, 2023), the IDF had made more than 12 million prerecorded phone calls, sent out more than 15 million texts, dropped more than 4.5 million leaflets, and placed more than 45,000 individual calls, “warning civilians to evacuate areas of hostilities and individual targets.” What other nation has ever made such efforts to spare civilian lives in the midst of a brutal war? This is the opposite of genocidal intent. As for the charge of starvation, according to Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories , more than 1 million metric tons of food entered Gaza between Oct. 7, 2023, and Jan. 17, 2025, alone. Based on the actual composition of the food entering Gaza, this represented roughly 2,600 calories per person per day. This does not mean that all the food actually reached the people, as there were massive distribution issues. But when it comes to intent, if you’re trying to wipe out a people group, you don’t make every effort to give them time to evacuate before bombing, nor do you send them food if you’re trying to starve them. All this is underscored by the fact that as many as 81% of the structures in Gaza were damaged or destroyed in the war, yet only 3% of the people were killed. And according to the IDF, at least 25,000 of those killed were Hamas combatants. There is also the issue of outright propaganda, with charges of “genocide” and “starvation” circulating before the Israeli offensive had even begun. As documented by NGO Monitor , on Oct. 9, 2023, just two days after the massacre, Al-Haq, Al Mezan and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights accused Israel of “employing starvation as a weapon.” On Oct. 11, Al-Haq said Israeli actions amounted to “acts of genocide.” By Oct. 15, the three groups were calling on states to protect Palestinians “against genocide” – still two weeks before the IDF’s ground invasion. Yet there’s more. Israel’s critics have raised the genocide charge against the Jewish state for decades, during which time the Palestinian population in Gaza and the West Bank has grown dramatically. In 2001, the Durban World Conference Against Racism NGO declaration called for investigation and prosecution of alleged “war crimes, acts of genocide and ethnic cleansing” by Israel. In 2008–09, U.N. General Assembly President Miguel d’Escoto Brockmann publicly said Israel’s actions raised the issue of genocide. In 2014, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas accused Israel at the U.N. of conducting a “war of genocide” against Palestinians in Gaza. Contrast all this rhetoric with the fact that in 1967, when Israel took control of Gaza, the population was between 400,000–440,000. Immediately before Oct. 7, 2023, the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics estimated 2,226,544 residents. This means that Gaza’s Palestinian population had grown by 400–450% – all while Israel was committing “genocide” against the people of Gaza! As for the West Bank, prior to the 1967 war, the population was estimated at 850,000. By 2023, PCBS estimated the population at 3,256,906 – approximately a fourfold population, or an increase of about 280%. Where was the genocide? Lastly, it has recently been revealed that, according to evidence released by the IDF , 170 Palestinians presented as journalists killed during the war were also operatives in Hamas, Islamic Jihad, or other terrorist organizations, while other Palestinian journalists have openly described Hamas intimidation , interference with content, threats and resulting self-censorship. In sum: 1) the number of deaths says there was no genocide; 2) there was no intent to commit genocide (quite the contrary); 3) the charge of genocide was used as a propaganda weapon before the war even began, not to mention in previous decades; and 4) much of the reporting from within Gaza was extremely biased, if not completely propagandistic. If the IDF committed war crimes, those must be investigated. The extremist voices within Israel must be countered. And the people of Gaza deserve compassion, with a path for a potentially better life. But, to say it once more, there was no genocide in Gaza. Enough with this perfidious lie.
